slides.title: Why words get split into pieces
slides.summary: Models read text as tokens. Common words are one token. Rarer words are split into reusable pieces.
body: A neural network can't read letters. It needs a fixed list of text pieces, called the vocabulary, where every piece has a number as its ID. Splitting text into those pieces is called tokenization. The big question is how big the pieces should be:

ul: Single letters: a tiny vocabulary, but every word turns into many tokens. Texts get long, and attention gets much slower as texts get longer (see Attention).
Whole words: short texts, but you'd need millions of entries, and every typo, name or new word would be unknown.
Parts of words: the middle ground everyone uses. Common words like "the" get one token. Rare words are built from common pieces: "unbelievable" becomes "un" + "believ" + "able".

body: Modern tokenizers work on raw bytes, not letters, so they can handle any text at all, including emoji, code and every language. Nothing is ever "unknown"; unusual text just uses more tokens.

body.note: Tokens are what you pay for and what limits are counted in. API prices, rate limits and context windows are all measured in tokens, not letters or words.

figure.alt: The sentence "I am learning tokenization" goes into a tokenizer, which checks a fixed vocabulary of about 128,000 pieces. It splits the text into five tokens: I, am, learning, token and ization, with the last word split in two. Each token becomes its row number in the vocabulary, so the model reads the list 40, 1097, 6975, 4037, 2065.
figure.caption: The whole journey in one picture: text goes in, the tokenizer splits it using the vocabulary, and the model only ever sees the ID numbers.

slides.title: How BPE builds the vocabulary
slides.summary: BPE builds a vocabulary by repeatedly joining the most common pair of neighbouring pieces.
body: Byte pair encoding (BPE) began as a way to compress files. Tokenizers use it because it finds the pieces that are common in real text by itself, without any grammar rules.

ul: Start with every word split into single bytes (shown here as letters).
Count how often each pair of neighbouring pieces appears in all the training text.
Join the most common pair into a new piece, and save that join as a rule.
Repeat until the vocabulary is big enough, usually 50,000 to 200,000 pieces.

body: Click Apply next merge. e and s sit next to each other most often, so they become es. Then es + t becomes est, and so on.
To split new text, break it into bytes and replay the saved joins in the same order. The same text always gives the same tokens.

body.note: The tokenizer is trained once, on its own, before the model. Then its vocabulary is locked, and the model learns one vector for each entry.

blocks.text: rule 0: start: every word split into characters

slides.title: Try a tokenizer
slides.summary: Play with a tokenizer to see why the number of tokens doesn't match the number of words.
body: This is a toy tokenizer that knows about 100 pieces. At each point in the text, it grabs the longest piece it knows. Real tokenizers like OpenAI's tiktoken and Google's SentencePiece know 50,000–200,000 pieces and use learned rules, but they behave in the same way.
Things to try:

ul: Misspell a word, like artifical. The tokenizer knows "artificial" as one piece, but the typo breaks into several smaller ones.
Remove the space before a word. The space in front is usually part of the token, so ␣learning and learning have different IDs and mean slightly different things to the model.
Type in another language. Pieces the vocabulary doesn't have fall back to single letters. So non-English text often needs more tokens to say the same thing, which also makes it cost more.

body.note: Models don't see letters. That's why tasks that seem easy, like counting the r's in "strawberry" or spelling a word backwards, have tripped models up. The word arrives as one or two ID numbers, not a row of letters.

viz.html: Small grey numbers are made-up token IDs. ␣ marks a leading space.

slides.title: Special tokens and chat templates
slides.summary: A chat is turned into one long line of tokens, with special tokens marking who is speaking.
body: Some vocabulary entries never come from normal text. These special tokens are signals the model learned in training: start of text, end of text, padding, and markers for each speaker in a chat (system, user, assistant).

A chat API takes your list of messages and lays them out using a chat template: every message in order, wrapped in speaker markers, as one long line of tokens. The model then writes the assistant's reply right after the last <|assistant|> marker.

ul: The system prompt isn't a separate input. It's just the first tokens in the line.
Each model family has its own template. Use the wrong one and the quality drops a lot, because the model never saw that format in training.
Good serving code turns a typed "<|user|>" into ordinary letters, not the special token, so a user can't pretend to be someone else.

body.note: It's like an HTTP request being turned into bytes to send over the network. The API gives you neat, structured messages; the model only ever sees the flattened version.

blocks.html: Amber = special tokens. The model writes its reply right after <|assistant|>. The exact names differ between model families.

slides.title: The embedding table
slides.summary: Each token ID is turned into a vector by looking up one row of a big learned table.
body: A token ID is just a label: the number 6975 says nothing about meaning. So the model's first real step swaps each ID for a list of d numbers (usually thousands) by looking it up in an embedding table.
The table is a matrix E with one row for each vocabulary entry, so its shape is [V, d]. Token 6975 picks row 6975. In code that's just an array lookup, so it costs almost nothing.

The numbers start out random. Training nudges them millions of times, until tokens used in similar ways have similar vectors. Unlike the fruit example in The big picture, no column means "sweetness". Meaning is spread across all d numbers, in ways researchers have to work hard to figure out.
Click a token on the right to see which row it selects.

body.note: The embedding table is learned along with everything else. In small models it's one of the biggest parts: GPT-2 small uses 38.6M of its 124M parameters here.

viz.html: GPT-2 small: 50,257 × 768 ≈ 38.6M parameters in this one table. Many models reuse it, flipped, as the output layer (called weight tying).

slides.title: What the positions of vectors mean
slides.summary: After training, similar words sit close together, and some relationships point in a consistent direction.
body: If you could plot the trained vectors, you'd see a pattern. Words with related meanings group together: fruits near fruits, programming languages near programming languages.

Some relationships even become consistent directions. Going from "man" to "woman" points roughly the same way as going from "king" to "queen". That's why the famous sum king − man + woman ≈ queen roughly works, first shown with word2vec in 2013.
Closeness is measured with cosine similarity, the same calculation as the fruit comparison in The big picture.

body.note: This is exactly how semantic search and RAG work. Turn every document into a vector once, turn the user's question into a vector, and return the documents whose vectors are closest. Vector databases exist to do this search quickly.

viz.html: A 2D sketch. Real embeddings have hundreds to thousands of dimensions, and these neat directions are only roughly true.

slides.title: Word order matters: adding position
slides.summary: Attention doesn't notice word order by itself, so position information has to be added.
body: Attention, the core step in the next chapter, compares every token with every other token. On its own it treats the input like a bag of words: shuffle the tokens and each one gets the same result. It can't tell "dog bites man" from "man bites dog".
So position has to be added in. The original Transformer (2017) added a fixed pattern of waves to each token's vector:

ul: Each pair of numbers goes up and down at a different speed, from very fast to very slow.
Together they give every position its own unique fingerprint.
Nearby positions get similar fingerprints, so the model can tell near from far.

body.note: Think of a clock with many hands. The second hand alone can't tell you the time. But seconds, minutes, hours and days together mark every moment uniquely, and moments close together look alike.

body: In the heatmap, each row is a position and each column is one number. The fast-changing columns are on the left and the slow ones on the right.

slides.title: RoPE: what modern models use
slides.summary: Modern models mark position by rotating vectors, so attention can directly see how far apart two tokens are.
body: Most current open models (Llama, Mistral, Qwen and others) use rotary position embeddings (RoPE) instead. Nothing is added to the token's vector. Instead, inside attention, the query and key vectors (next chapter) are rotated by an angle that grows with the token's position.

Why rotate? Attention scores two tokens with a dot product, and the dot product depends on the angle between the two vectors. Rotate one by position m and the other by position n, and the angle between them only depends on m − n: how far apart they are.
Try it: move both sliders by the same amount. Both arrows turn, but the angle between them, and so the score, doesn't change.

body.note: RoPE tells the model relative position ("three tokens back"), not absolute position ("token 1,207"). That suits language, where nearby words usually matter most. It's also one reason context windows can be made longer after training.

code: q, k = rope(q, m), rope(k, n)   # then q·k as usual

slides.title: The input is now a matrix
slides.summary: The input stage ends with one vector per token. This is the residual stream that every later layer reads and updates.
body: Put the steps together: split the text into tokens, look up each token's vector, and add position. The result is a matrix with one row per token and d columns: shape [n, d], or [B, n, d] for a batch.
This matrix is called the residual stream, and it's the star of the rest of the course. Every later layer reads from it and adds its own bit back.

body.note: The shape stays the same all the way through the model until the very end. That's why you can stack 32, 80 or 120 identical layers: each takes [B, n, d] in and gives [B, n, d] out.

body: Each coloured square on the right is one number. Real rows have thousands.
